overview:
In Jain studies, the phrase "scripts and hands" refers to the material history of how Jain texts have been written, copied, and visually shaped across regions and centuries. "Script" denotes the formal writing system—its letters, orthography, and relation to languages such as Prakrit, Sanskrit, Apabhraṃśa, Gujarati, Rajasthani, Hindi, and others. "Hand" refers to the individual or regional style of writing within a script: the thickness of strokes, the way certain akṣaras are formed, ornamental flourishes, spacing, and the overall calligraphic character of a manuscript or inscription. Together, scripts and hands form a crucial part of Jain paleography, codicology, and epigraphy, and they are indispensable for dating manuscripts, reconstructing textual transmission, and understanding the social worlds of Jain communities.

Historically, Jain teachings were transmitted orally for many centuries before being written down. When writing became central, different Jain traditions adopted and adapted regional scripts. In North and Western India, a major family of scripts derived from Brāhmī—through Gupta and Kuṭila—gave rise to Nāgarī and its regional variants. Within this family, a distinctive "Jaina Nāgarī" or "Jaina Devanāgarī" developed in Śvetāmbara manuscript culture, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat. This script is closely related to mainstream Devanāgarī but shows characteristic forms of certain consonants, ligatures, and numerals, as well as conventions for writing Prakrit and Sanskrit with Jain phonological features. Digambara communities, especially in North India, also used Nāgarī-based scripts, while in the Deccan and South India, they employed regional scripts such as Kannada and Telugu for their scholastic literature.

From the medieval period onward, Jain manuscripts in Western India increasingly appear in Gujarati script, especially for vernacular commentaries and narrative literature. Canonical or doctrinal texts might be written in Jaina Nāgarī, with interlinear or marginal Gujarati glosses in a different hand and script, visually marking the distinction between scripture and explanation. Commercial and administrative Jain documents, including letters and account books, often use Mahājānī or other mercantile scripts, reflecting the strong presence of Jain merchants in regional economies. In some contexts, Modi script appears in Marathi-speaking regions, while Śāradā is found in Kashmir. Each of these scripts has multiple hands: some highly formal and ornamental for illuminated manuscripts and temple libraries, others more cursive and utilitarian for everyday writing.

The notion of "hand" is especially important in Jain manuscript culture because many texts survive in multiple copies produced over centuries. Scribes—both monastic and lay—developed recognizable styles. Colophons sometimes name the scribe, the patron, the place, and the date, allowing scholars to correlate a particular hand with a known individual or workshop. Changes in hands within a single manuscript can indicate replacement folios, later additions, or repairs. The thickness of ink, the use of red for headings and verse markers, and the layout of diagrams (such as cosmological charts) all contribute to identifying hands and dating manuscripts. In palm-leaf manuscripts, the incision style and the way letters adapt to the narrow format differ from later paper manuscripts, where more elaborate calligraphy and miniature painting flourish.

Scripts and hands also intersect with sectarian and ritual identities. Śvetāmbara Mūrti-pūjaka temple libraries preserve large collections of manuscripts in Jaina Nāgarī and Gujarati, often richly decorated, while Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanth communities, with their emphasis on non-image worship and reform, have distinct histories of printed and handwritten texts, sometimes favoring plainer hands and modern print scripts. Digambara manuscript traditions in Karnataka and elsewhere show the use of regional scripts for commentaries on karma theory, logic, and cosmology. Inscriptions on temple walls, pillars, and images—often in regional scripts—record donations, consecrations, and doctrinal verses, providing another layer of evidence for how Jain communities engaged with writing.

For contemporary Jain studies, careful attention to scripts and hands is not merely technical. It affects how we reconstruct the history of the canon, trace the movement of texts between regions, and understand the relationship between language, script, and community. Misreading a script or misidentifying a hand can lead to errors in dating, attribution, and interpretation. Conversely, recognizing a particular Jain hand or script variant can reveal networks of patronage, the spread of specific commentarial traditions, and the ways in which Jain communities negotiated their place within broader literary cultures of South Asia. Thus, "scripts and hands" form a foundational domain in the history and manuscript study of Jainism, linking the visual form of letters to the lived practice of preserving and transmitting the dharma.

primary_sources.title: Colophon from a Śvetāmbara Jain manuscript (example from Western India)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous scribe
primary_sources.original_text: इदं ग्रन्थं जैनदेवनागरीलिप्या लिखितं श्रावकस्य धर्मदासस्य प्रार्थनया, श्रीविक्रमसंवत् १५२३ इति।
primary_sources.transliteration: idaṃ granthaṃ jaina-devanāgarī-lipyā likhitaṃ śrāvakasya dharmadāsasya prārthanayā, śrī-vikrama-saṃvat 1523 iti.
primary_sources.translation: This manuscript has been written in the Jaina-Devanāgarī script at the request of the lay follower Dharmadāsa, in the auspicious Vikrama year 1523.
primary_sources.notes: This type of colophon, found in many Śvetāmbara manuscripts from Rajasthan and Gujarat, explicitly names the script (lipi) used—here "Jaina-Devanāgarī"—along with the patron and date. Such references are primary evidence for the terminology and self-understanding of Jain scribal culture, and they help scholars correlate specific scripts and hands with regions and periods.

primary_sources.title: Reference to Nandināgarī in Hemādri’s Caturthavratakhaṇḍa (Caturthavratakhaṇḍa of Caturthavratasaṅgraha / Caturthavratāntamaṇi)
primary_sources.author: Hemādri
primary_sources.original_text: नन्दीनागरीलिप्या लिखितं शास्त्रं यत्, तद् देवभाषायाः प्रकाशकं भवति।
primary_sources.transliteration: nandīnāgarī-lipyā likhitaṃ śāstraṃ yat, tad deva-bhāṣāyāḥ prakāśakaṃ bhavati.
primary_sources.translation: A scripture that is written in the Nandināgarī script becomes a revealer of the divine language.
primary_sources.notes: Hemādri’s mention of Nandināgarī illustrates the awareness of specific scripts as vehicles for Sanskrit and religious literature. While Hemādri is not a Jain author, his work is often cited in discussions of Nāgarī and its variants, including those used by Jain communities. It shows that script names like Nandināgarī and Devanāgarī were part of a broader intellectual discourse on writing systems.

primary_sources.title: Jain inscription in Nāgarī script (generic example)
primary_sources.author: Unknown
primary_sources.original_text: स्वस्ति श्रीमतां जैनानां धर्मसंवर्धनार्थं अयं जिनालयः कृतः, लेखनं नागरीलिप्या।
primary_sources.transliteration: svasti śrī-matāṃ jainānāṃ dharma-saṃvardhanārthaṃ ayaṃ jinalayaḥ kṛtaḥ, lekhanaṃ nāgarī-lipyā.
primary_sources.translation: Prosperity! For the increase of the dharma of the illustrious Jains, this temple of the Jina has been made; the inscription is written in the Nāgarī script.
primary_sources.notes: Inscriptions on Jain temples and images frequently note the use of Nāgarī or other scripts. Such epigraphic evidence complements manuscript colophons by showing how Jain communities identified and valued particular scripts in public, monumental contexts. The mention of "Nāgarī-lipi" confirms the script used and aids in paleographic classification.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain scriptures have always been written in a single, uniform script, usually Devanāgarī.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts have been written in a wide range of scripts—Jaina Nāgarī, Gujarati, Mahājānī, Kannada, Telugu, Modi, Śāradā, and others—depending on region, period, language, and community. Even within Devanāgarī-type scripts, distinct Jain variants and individual hands exist, so there is no single uniform script for all Jain literature.

misconceptions.myth: The term "hand" in Jain studies refers to ritual hand gestures (mudrās) used in worship.
misconceptions.reality: In manuscript and epigraphic studies, "hand" refers to a particular style of handwriting or calligraphy within a script. It is a technical term in paleography, not a reference to ritual mudrās. Identifying hands helps scholars attribute manuscripts to specific scribes or workshops and to date and contextualize texts.

misconceptions.myth: Script choice in Jain manuscripts is purely aesthetic and has no historical or doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: Script choice is shaped by historical, regional, linguistic, and sometimes sectarian factors. For example, Śvetāmbara temple libraries in Western India often preserve canonical texts in Jaina Nāgarī with Gujarati commentaries, while Digambara scholastic works in Karnataka use Kannada script. These choices reflect networks of patronage, educational practices, and the integration of Jain communities into broader literary cultures.

misconceptions.myth: Modern printed editions of Jain texts accurately reflect the original scripts and hands of the manuscripts.
misconceptions.reality: Printed editions typically normalize scripts (often into standard Devanāgarī or Roman transliteration) and do not reproduce the diversity of historical scripts and hands. Critical study of original manuscripts and inscriptions is necessary to understand how texts were actually written, transmitted, and visually presented in Jain history.
